conversation.content: Let's design a search engine platform — not just a single search application, but a reusable search infrastructure that multiple teams across the organization can build on. What questions do you have?

Great problem. A few things I'd want to clarify. First, what's the scope of 'search' — are we talking full-text document search, structured data search, or both? Second, how many internal teams would consume this platform, and what's the diversity of their data — are they all indexing similar document types or wildly different schemas? Third, what's our expected index size and query throughput? And finally, do we need real-time indexing or is near-real-time acceptable?

Both full-text and structured. About 30 teams with very different data — product catalog, support tickets, user profiles, log data. Total index size around 50TB across all tenants. 20,000 queries per second at peak. Near-real-time indexing is fine — under 5 seconds from write to searchable. Go ahead.

Got it. Before I dive into architecture, let me frame the platform boundaries. There are three user personas: the platform team that operates the infrastructure, the developer teams that integrate via APIs, and the end users who search through their team's applications. Each persona has different needs. The platform team cares about operational cost and multi-tenant isolation. Developer teams care about ease of integration, a powerful query DSL, and relevance tuning. End users just want fast, relevant results. I'll design around all three.
That's a mature framing. Let's start with the indexing side. How does data get into the platform?

I'd expose an Indexing API with two modes. First, a synchronous REST API for low-volume, real-time indexing — POST /v1/indices/{index_name}/documents. Second, a bulk ingestion path via Kafka. Teams publish documents to a tenant-specific Kafka topic, and our indexing workers consume and index them. Each document goes through a pipeline: schema validation, field extraction, analyzers and tokenizers, then into the search engine. Underneath I'd use Elasticsearch clusters, but the API abstracts that away — teams don't know or care about the underlying engine.
You mentioned schema validation. How do you handle the fact that 30 teams have wildly different document schemas?

Each tenant registers a schema for their index through our management API. The schema defines field names, types — text, keyword, numeric, date, geo_point — and analysis settings per field, like which tokenizer or stemmer to use. We store schemas in a schema registry backed by PostgreSQL with versioning. When a document arrives, we validate against the registered schema. For schema evolution, we support additive changes — new fields — without downtime. Breaking changes like type changes require creating a new index version and reindexing, which we automate with a blue-green index swap.
Good. Now let's talk about the query side. You mentioned a query DSL — what does that look like?

The query DSL is a JSON-based language that abstracts over Elasticsearch's query DSL while being simpler and more opinionated. It supports: match queries for full-text search with configurable fuzziness, filter clauses for exact matches on structured fields, range queries for numeric and date fields, boolean combinations with must/should/must_not, and faceted aggregations for building filter UIs. For example, a product catalog team could write a query that combines a text match on product name with a filter on category and a price range, plus a facet aggregation on brand. We translate this DSL into Elasticsearch queries server-side, which lets us optimize and evolve the underlying implementation without breaking clients.
How do teams tune relevance? A product search has very different ranking needs than a support ticket search.

Relevance tuning is the biggest differentiator for a search platform. I'd build a relevance tuning dashboard where each team can configure: field boost weights — title matches score higher than body matches; custom scoring functions — for example, boosting newer products or popular support articles; synonym dictionaries per index; and query-time signal injection — like personalization signals. Under the hood, these configurations translate to Elasticsearch function_score queries and custom analyzers. The dashboard also provides an A/B testing framework — teams can run two relevance configurations side by side, measure click-through rate and mean reciprocal rank, and promote the winner. All without deploying code.
Excellent. Now, multi-tenant isolation is critical. How do you prevent one noisy tenant from degrading the experience for others?

Multi-tenant isolation operates at multiple layers. At the cluster level, I'd tier tenants by SLA. High-throughput, latency-sensitive tenants like product search get dedicated Elasticsearch clusters. Medium-tier tenants share a cluster but get dedicated indices with isolated shards. Low-volume tenants share indices with routing-based isolation. At the query layer, each tenant gets a query rate limit and a circuit breaker. If a tenant sends an expensive query that would consume disproportionate resources — like a wildcard leading query — we have query cost estimation that rejects queries exceeding a cost threshold. At the indexing layer, each tenant gets a dedicated Kafka partition group with configurable throughput limits. We also have per-tenant resource quotas: maximum index size, maximum shard count, and maximum query complexity.
What happens when a tenant exceeds their quota? Walk me through the failure mode.

Graduated response. First, soft limits — when a tenant hits 80% of their index size quota, we emit a warning via webhook and dashboard notification. Their platform contact gets an email. Second, at 100%, new indexing requests return 429 with a Retry-After header indicating when capacity might free up. Existing indexed data remains fully searchable — we never degrade read availability for a quota issue. Third, for query rate limits, we use a token bucket per tenant. Excess queries get queued briefly — 100ms — then shed with 429 if the bucket doesn't refill. The key principle: one tenant's write overload never impacts another tenant's reads. We enforce this through physical isolation of the hot path — each tenant's query traffic is routed through a dedicated thread pool in the query service, so one slow tenant can't exhaust the connection pool for others.
Let's talk about the operational side. With 50TB of index data across 30 teams, how do you handle capacity planning and cluster operations?

Capacity planning is a continuous process. I'd build an internal capacity model that tracks per-tenant metrics: index size growth rate, query rate trends, and p99 latency. We project forward 90 days and alert if any cluster is forecast to exceed 70% disk or CPU utilization. For cluster operations, I'd use an infrastructure-as-code approach — each cluster configuration lives in a Git repo, and changes go through PR review. Scaling operations like adding data nodes or rebalancing shards are automated via an operator pattern — a control plane service monitors cluster health and triggers automated actions: rebalancing shards when a node is hot, scaling up when queue depth exceeds thresholds, and performing rolling restarts during version upgrades. We expose a platform health dashboard showing cluster utilization per tier, query latency distributions, and indexing throughput.
An entire Elasticsearch cluster goes down for one of the tiers. What's your recovery strategy?

For the dedicated high-tier clusters, I'd run cross-cluster replication to a warm standby in a different availability zone. Failover is semi-automated — our monitoring detects the failure, pages on-call, and the operator can initiate failover with a single command that updates the query routing layer to point to the standby. RPO is near-zero since replication is continuous. RTO target is under 5 minutes. For shared clusters, the Elasticsearch replica shards provide intra-cluster resilience. If we lose a full cluster, we rebuild from snapshots stored in S3. We take hourly snapshots, so worst-case RPO is one hour of data. However, since we have the source-of-truth data in the upstream systems and Kafka retention, we can fully reindex from source. I'd have a 'rebuild from source' runbook that triggers a full reindex from each tenant's Kafka topic — we retain 7 days of messages for exactly this purpose.
How do you handle the developer experience side? Onboarding a new team to the platform.

Developer experience is what makes or breaks a platform. The onboarding flow: a team creates a project through our self-service portal, which provisions a namespace, API keys, and a sandbox index. They define their schema through the portal's schema editor, which validates and previews analyzer behavior — you can type in sample text and see how it tokenizes. We provide SDKs in Python, Java, Go, and TypeScript that wrap our REST API with type-safe query builders. The sandbox comes pre-loaded with synthetic data matching their schema so they can test queries immediately. Documentation lives alongside the portal — interactive API explorer with runnable examples. The typical onboarding time target is under one day from signup to first query in production.
One team complains that their search results are terrible — users aren't finding what they're looking for. How do you help them diagnose and fix this?

First, we need data. The platform collects search quality signals: queries with zero results, queries where users don't click any result, queries where users click but immediately bounce back, and queries where users refine their search terms. We surface these in a search analytics dashboard per tenant. For diagnosis, we have a query explain tool — you input a query and a document, and it shows the full scoring breakdown: which fields matched, what boost was applied, why document A ranked above document B. This is built on Elasticsearch's explain API but presented in a human-readable format. For fixes, the relevance tuning dashboard I mentioned earlier lets them adjust field weights, add synonyms, and boost signals. We also offer office hours where the platform team pairs with product teams on relevance tuning — this knowledge transfer is critical for platform adoption.
Let's discuss the query processing pipeline in more detail. A query comes in — walk me through every step before results are returned.

The query pipeline has six stages. One: authentication and tenant identification from the API key. Two: query parsing and validation — we parse the DSL, validate field names against the tenant's schema, and estimate query cost. Three: query rewriting — we expand synonyms, apply spelling correction using a did-you-mean model trained on the tenant's query logs, and apply any tenant-configured query rules like redirects for specific terms. Four: translation to Elasticsearch query — we combine the rewritten query with the tenant's relevance configuration including boosts, function scores, and filters. Five: execution — we route to the correct cluster and index, execute with a timeout, and collect results. Six: post-processing — we apply any result-time transformations like highlighting, snippet extraction, and facet count computation. The whole pipeline target is under 100ms for p95. Each stage emits timing metrics so we can identify bottlenecks.
At 20,000 QPS, how do you ensure this six-stage pipeline stays under 100ms?

Several strategies. First, stages 1-3 are CPU-bound and operate on small data — they're sub-millisecond. The expensive part is stage 5, the Elasticsearch query. For that: we size clusters so that each shard handles a bounded number of documents — no more than 30GB per shard — keeping query latency predictable. We use query result caches at the platform layer for identical queries within a short TTL — many search UIs repeat the same queries from different users. We warm the filesystem cache on Elasticsearch nodes by running common queries after restarts. For tail latency, we use hedged requests — if a query hasn't returned within p50 latency, we send a duplicate to a replica shard. The first response wins. This dramatically cuts p99 at the cost of a small increase in total query volume. Finally, the cost estimation in stage 2 rejects pathologically expensive queries — no leading wildcards, no unbounded aggregations — before they reach Elasticsearch.
How would you measure success of this platform overall? What metrics would you report to leadership?

I'd report on three categories. Adoption metrics: number of teams onboarded, total queries per day, and trend — is the platform growing? Time-to-onboard for new teams — target under one day. Reliability metrics: platform availability — target 99.95%, indexing lag p99 — target under 5 seconds, query latency p99 — target under 200ms. Efficiency metrics: cost per million queries — this is the platform's unit economics. Infrastructure cost growth rate versus query volume growth rate — if queries grow 3x but cost only grows 2x, we're showing economies of scale. And a qualitative metric: developer NPS from a quarterly survey. If teams love the platform, they'll advocate for it internally, which drives adoption without our team doing sales.
We're running out of time. Any final thoughts on what you'd prioritize for the first version?

For V1, I'd focus on the narrowest useful platform. Indexing API with schema registration, the query DSL covering the 80% use case — match, filter, sort, paginate — and basic multi-tenancy with index-level isolation. I'd skip the relevance tuning dashboard, the A/B testing, and the advanced query rewriting. Instead I'd onboard two design partners — one high-volume team and one low-volume team — validate the API design with real usage, then iterate. The biggest risk isn't technical; it's building a platform nobody uses because the API is clunky or the onboarding is painful. So I'd invest heavily in documentation and SDKs from day one.
Excellent interview. You demonstrated strong platform thinking with deep technical grounding. Thank you.

strengths: Exceptional platform framing — identified three distinct user personas and designed around each
Deep multi-tenant isolation strategy with graduated enforcement and physical isolation
Strong developer experience focus with concrete onboarding flow and tooling
weaknesses: Could have done more explicit capacity estimation — disk, memory, CPU per cluster
Didn't discuss data modeling or schema design tradeoffs in depth beyond the registry
